title: Holding more than it should
question: How can a solution hold more solute than it normally could?
hook: Some solutions sit holding extra solute, until one tiny crystal sets it all off.
idea: A supersaturated solution holds more solute than equilibrium allows and releases the excess once something starts crystals forming.

beats.prompt: A solution cools but stays clear, though it holds more solute than it should. A tiny crystal of the solute is dropped in. What happens?

choices.label: Crystals begin to form around it
The tiny crystal simply dissolves and nothing changes
choices.feedback: Adding a tiny crystal of the solute is the common way to overcome the barrier to forming crystals.

choices.label: The extra solute escapes as a gas
choices.feedback: The excess solute separates from the solution as crystals, not as a gas.

beats.explain: The tiny crystal acts as a starting site, so the excess solute can separate out as crystals.

beats.prompt: Put the steps of recrystallization in order.
items: Heat the impure compound with solvent until it dissolves
Filter off any solid impurity that remains
Lower the temperature so the solution briefly becomes supersaturated
The compound crystallizes out, leaving impurities in the liquid
beats.explain: The compound is dissolved hot, cleaned of solids, cooled into supersaturation, then crystallizes while impurities stay dissolved.

beats.prompt: Match each method to what it does.
pairs: Adding a tiny crystal of the solute
Releases particles that act as nucleation centres
Separates crystals from the liquid in industry
beats.explain: Each of these either starts crystals forming or uses crystals to separate and purify a compound.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: A hot solution is cooled, and in most cases solubility decreases with decreasing temperature.
So at the lower temperature the solution can hold more solute than it should.
A thermodynamic barrier can stop crystals forming, so the solution may stay supersaturated.
So adding a tiny crystal of the solute would only dissolve and change nothing.
beats.explain: Adding a tiny crystal of the solute, called seeding, is the common way to overcome the barrier and start crystals forming.
